L0: # Zero Knowledge (About) Encryption
L1: 
L2: A Comparative Security Analysis of Three Cloud-based Password Managers
L3: 
L4: Matteo Scarlata, Giovanni Torrisi, Matilda Backendal, Kenneth G. Paterson
L5: 
L6: ETH Zurich & Università della Svizzera italiana (USI)
L7: 
L8: 【0†Read the full paper (ePrint)†eprint.iacr.org】
L9: 
L10: To appear at USENIX Security ’26
L11: ## Overview
L12: 
L13: Cloud-based password managers help users store and manage their credentials by encrypting them into a vault protected by a single master password. Leading vendors market this as Zero Knowledge Encryption, conveying the idea that the server storing the vault cannot learn anything about its contents – even if the server is compromised.
L14: We put this to the test. Analysing the three leading password managers that make the "Zero Knowledge Encryption" claim – Bitwarden, LastPass, and Dashlane, collectively serving over 60 million users and holding approximately 23% market share – plus an additional analysis of 1Password, we find 27 distinct attacks that a malicious server can mount against their users. The attacks range in severity from integrity violations to the complete compromise of all vaults in an organisation.
L15: The majority of the attacks allow the recovery of passwords.
L16: ## Am I Impacted? What Should I Do?
L17: 
L18: Don't stop using password managers! Using a password manager is probably the single most effective action you can take to strengthen your security.
L19: 
L20: No need to panic: all of our attacks presume a malicious server. We have no reason to believe that the password manager vendors are currently malicious or compromised, and as long as things stay that way, your passwords are safe. That said, password managers are high-value targets, and breaches do happen.
L21: If you use Bitwarden, LastPass, Dashlane or 1Password
L22: 
L23: You can check remediation status in the Ethical Considerations section of our paper and the responses of the password managers at the following links: 【1†Bitwarden†bitwarden.com】, 【2†Dashlane†dashlane.com】 (【3†advisory†support.dashlane.com】), 【4†LastPass†blog.lastpass.com】, 【5†1Password†1password.com】.
L24: 
L25: If you use a different password manager
L26: 
L27: You can ask your provider the following questions:
L28:   1. Do you offer end-to-end encryption? What security do you provide in case your server infrastructure were to be compromised?
L29:   2. How do you check that public keys and public-key ciphertexts are authentic?
L30:   3. How do you authenticate security-critical settings, such as the KDF type and the iteration count?
L31:   4. Do you provide integrity guarantees for a user's vault as a whole? Can a malicious server add items to your vault?
L32: You can also ask your favourite password manager to commission an audit checking for our attacks in their products.
L33: 
L34: * * *
L35: ## The Password Managers
L36: 
L37: We analyse four prominent cloud-based password managers, each of which claims to implement Zero Knowledge Encryption.
L38: ### 【6†Image: Bitwarden logo】【7†Image: Bitwarden logo】
L39: An open-source password manager founded in 2016, counting 10 million users, 50,000 business customers and 11% market share. Bitwarden is the only product we study which allows self-hosting. It uses AES-CBC-HMAC for authenticated encryption of data in the vault. Fields in vault items (username, password, url, ...) are encrypted separately: a malicious server could carry out cut-and-paste attacks and leak metadata.

L31: ### 【17†Zero Knowledge (About) Encryption: A Comparative Security Analysis of Four Cloud-based Password Managers】
L32: 
L33: Matteo Scarlata, ETH Zurich
L34: 
L35: Giovanni Torrisi, Universita della Svizzera Italiana
L36: 
L37: Matilda Backendal, Universita della Svizzera Italiana
L38: 
L39: Kenneth G. Paterson, ETH Zurich
L40: ##### Abstract
L41: Zero Knowledge Encryption is a term widely used by vendors of cloud-based password managers. Although it has no strict technical meaning, the term conveys the idea that the server, who stores encrypted password vaults on behalf of users, is unable to learn anything about the contents of those vaults. The security claims made by vendors imply that this should hold even if the server is fully malicious.
L42: This threat model is justified in practice by the high sensitivity of vault data, which makes password manager servers an attractive target for breaches (as evidenced by a history of attacks). We examine the extent to which security against a fully malicious server holds true for four leading vendors who make the Zero Knowledge Encryption claim: Bitwarden, LastPass, Dashlane and 1Password. Collectively, they have more than 60 million users and 23% market share.
L43: We present 12 distinct attacks against Bitwarden, 7 against LastPass, 6 against Dashlane and 6 against 1Password. The attacks range in severity, from integrity violations of targeted user vaults to the complete compromise of all the vaults associated with an organisation. The majority of the attacks allow recovery of passwords. We have disclosed our findings to the vendors and remediation is underway.
L44: Our attacks showcase the importance of considering the malicious server threat model for cloud-based password managers. Despite vendors’ attempts to achieve security in this setting, we uncover several common design anti-patterns and cryptographic misconceptions that resulted in vulnerabilities. We discuss possible mitigations and also reflect more broadly on what can be learned from our analysis by developers of end-to-end encrypted systems.
L45: Note: This is the full version of a paper published at USENIX Security '26. It includes all the attacks and additional results on 1Password.
